title: “Implement the Wage Code and Social Security Code immediately”
author: Editorial Desk
summary: The 159th Kendriya Karya Samithi met in Bhopal on 22-24 August 2025. What the Wage and Social Security Codes do, what BMS asked, and what followed in November 2025.
body:
*Photo: 159th Kendriya Karya Samithi, August 2025*

From **22 to 24 August 2025**, the **159th Kendriya Karya Samithi (Central Executive Council)** of the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh met in Bhopal. At the end of the three days it issued a statement urging the Union Government to **implement the Wage Code and the Social Security Code immediately**. The meeting adopted three resolutions. It was chaired by BMS President Hiranmay Pandya and conducted by General Secretary Ravindra Himte. This post explains what the two Codes are, why BMS singled them out, what else the meeting decided, and what followed.

## Where the Codes came from

India has had a large number of central labour laws, many of them passed between the 1930s and the 1950s. Over several years the Government worked on merging 29 of them into four Codes: the Code on Wages, the Industrial Relations Code, the Code on Social Security and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code. The Code on Wages was passed in 2019 and the other three in 2020, but for years, passing a law did not mean it applied. Each Code needed a notification bringing it into force and rules under it, and the Centre and States each had to frame their own.

That was the position in August 2025. The Codes were on the statute book but not in effect, and workers were still governed by the old laws. This is the background to BMS's demand.

## Why BMS singled out two of the four

The BMS statement described the Wage Code and the Social Security Code as the Codes that are more beneficial for ordinary workers, and said that BMS had consistently pressed for their immediate implementation. In its view they should not wait for the other two.

- The **Code on Wages** brings the legal protection of minimum wages to all workers and provides for a **national floor wage**, set by the Central Government, below which no State may fix its minimum wage except in limited cases. It replaces four laws: the Payment of Wages Act, the Minimum Wages Act, the Payment of Bonus Act and the Equal Remuneration Act.
- The **Code on Social Security** brings together laws on provident fund, health insurance, gratuity, maternity benefit and workers' compensation, among others, and for the first time defines gig work, platform work and aggregators in statute. Aggregators are required to contribute a percentage of their turnover, between 1 and 2 per cent and capped at 5 per cent of what they pay to such workers, and an Aadhaar-linked account number is meant to make benefits portable from one State to another.

BMS's reasoning was straightforward. Delay in notification means that these provisions, which the law-makers had already approved, were being denied to people who had waited for years. A security guard on a minimum wage that is not enforced, a delivery rider with no social security cover, and a contract worker who has no gratuity do not gain anything from a law that is not in force.

## What BMS said about the other two Codes

The same statement did not give a blanket welcome to the entire package. According to the Organiser report of the meeting, BMS opposes the Industrial Relations Code and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, because of clauses that it considers harmful to workers' interests. It asked the Government to implement the Codes in phases and in consultation with tripartite partners, and said that all four should not be rushed. This is a consistent BMS position, to support what is beneficial, to object to what is not, and to ask for dialogue before rules are finalised.

## The Indian Labour Conference

The meeting also asked the Labour Ministry to convene the **Indian Labour Conference (ILC)**, its highest tripartite body, as early as possible. BMS noted that the ILC last met in 2015, and that the world of work has changed greatly since then, through technology and digital transition. A conference with government, employers and workers in the same room is where a controversial question, such as how a floor wage should be fixed or what counts as a platform worker, can be discussed before it reaches the stage of a dispute.

## The rest of the meeting

The Karya Samithi dealt with other matters as well, which gives an idea of its range.

- It welcomed the Haryana Government's decision to regularise contract workers under the Kaushal Vikas Yojana, and thanked the Chief Minister.
- It raised concern about the **Face Recognition System** introduced under the ICDS scheme by the Women and Child Welfare Ministry, saying that it causes practical difficulties for Anganwadi workers and is used by district officials to harass them, and demanded that it be withdrawn.
- It decided to hold BMS's 20th All-India Conference in Puri in the first week of February 2026, with about 2,500 delegates from 42 industrial federations and 28 State units.

## How BMS works

The Kendriya Karya Samithi is the central working body of BMS. It meets several times a year, reviews the situation and passes resolutions that become the basis of demands to the Government, memoranda and, at times, nationwide programmes. A resolution of this kind is seldom the end of the matter. It is followed by letters, meetings with the Labour Minister and, where BMS thinks it necessary, demonstrations by its units across the country.

## What followed

On **21 November 2025**, the Government brought the four Codes into force, consolidating 29 laws. The Ministry's announcement said that, among other things, minimum wage protection would cover all workers, appointment letters would be compulsory, fixed-term employees would be eligible for gratuity after one year and not five, and social security coverage, which it put at about 19 per cent of the workforce in 2015, had risen to more than 64 per cent in 2025. Law firms noted that the old Acts' rules would continue in transition until fresh rules were made, and that many States had only draft rules, so that implementation would be uneven.

The BMS website records that BMS welcomed the implementation of the Codes, and that its delegations met the Labour Minister, Dr Mansukh Mandaviya, on pending issues. BMS's triennial convention in Puri, Odisha, later elected S. Mallesham as President and Surendra Kumar Pandey as General Secretary.

## What remains to be done

The notification is not the end of the work. Rules have to be framed in every State, workers have to be told about their rights, and registration of gig and platform workers has to be done. BMS's other demands, including the holding of the ILC, the removal of provisions in the Industrial Relations Code it objects to, and the protection of Anganwadi and other scheme workers, remain on the table. The first test of the Codes will be whether a worker who has never been covered by a law finds that it now applies to her.
